prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that the library's decline is poorly understood?

choices.text: the statement that we know less than we would like about how the library declined
choices.rationale: Correct. This statement directly expresses limited knowledge of the decline.

choices.text: the statement that scholars came from distant lands to read, argue, and write
choices.rationale: Visiting scholars do not address the decline.

choices.text: the statement that scrolls aboard docking ships were searched and then copied
choices.rationale: Copying scrolls concerns growth, not decline.

choices.text: the statement that the collection may have held several hundred thousand scrolls in all
choices.rationale: Collection size does not address the decline.

explanation: The uncertainty claim is stated directly in that sentence.

stimulus.title: A House for Every Book
stimulus.text: The ancient library at Alexandria aimed at something audacious: to gather a copy of every book in the world. Ships docking at the harbor were searched, and any scrolls aboard were copied; sometimes the library kept the original and returned the copy. Scholars from distant lands came to read, argue, and write, and the collection may have held hundreds of thousands of scrolls. We know less than we would like about how the library declined, and popular stories of a single great fire oversimplify a slow loss across centuries. Still, the idea behind it endured. The dream of one place that holds all knowledge has reappeared, in new forms, ever since.

prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that some folk weather signs had real value?

choices.text: the statement that much of the folk knowledge mixed in superstition
choices.rationale: The superstition detail shows the unreliable side, not the value.

choices.text: the statement that the conditions producing a hazy moon truly can precede rain
choices.rationale: Correct. The hazy-moon-precedes-rain detail shows a folk sign with a real basis.

choices.text: the statement that satellites now map storms from orbit
choices.rationale: Satellite mapping describes modern tools, not folk-sign value.

choices.text: the statement that such clues were gathered into almanacs and passed down
choices.rationale: Gathering clues into almanacs concerns how they spread, not their accuracy.

explanation: Real value is supported by the hazy-moon-precedes-rain detail.

stimulus.title: Reading the Weather Before Radio
stimulus.text: Long before satellites mapped storms from orbit, farmers learned to read the sky and the land for signs of coming weather. A ring of haze around the moon, the smell of soil before rain, the behavior of swallows flying low: such clues were gathered into almanacs and passed down through families. Much of this folk knowledge was unreliable, mixing keen observation with superstition. Yet some of it held real wisdom, since the conditions that produce a hazy moon truly can precede rain. Modern forecasting has not so much replaced this older watching as absorbed its best parts, trading the rooster's crow for the radar's sweep.

prompt: Which quotation best supports the idea that the narrator's early failures stemmed from impatience?

choices.text: 'she believed in watching'
choices.rationale: This describes Mrs. Delgado's method.

choices.text: 'mostly because nobody else would'
choices.rationale: This explains why the narrator took the shift, not why the loaves failed.

choices.text: 'instead of until I got bored'
choices.rationale: Correct. The narrator had been ending the rest when boredom set in rather than when the dough was ready.

choices.text: 'The loaf that came out that day was not perfect'
choices.rationale: This concerns the improved loaf, not the cause of the earlier failures.

explanation: The admission that proofing ended with boredom shows the impatience behind the flat loaves.

stimulus.title: Proof
stimulus.text: The summer I was sixteen, I worked the four a.m. shift at Delgado's, mostly because nobody else would. Mrs. Delgado did not believe in teaching; she believed in watching. For two weeks I shaped loaves beside her while she said nothing, and for two weeks my loaves came out of the oven squat and sullen, like they resented being made. Then one morning she pressed a finger into my dough, frowned, and said, 'You are in a hurry. Bread is not.' That was all. I slowed down. I let the dough rest in the proof box until it had nearly doubled, instead of until I got bored. The loaf that came out that day was not perfect, but it rose. I have thought about that sentence more often than anything I learned in school, mostly when I am about to rush something that will not be rushed.

prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that sleep aids memory?

choices.text: the statement that, during deep sleep, waves of electrical activity sweep across the cortex
choices.rationale: The waves describe a mechanism, not the memory outcome.

choices.text: the finding that students who slept after studying recalled more words than those kept awake
choices.rationale: Correct. The comparison of sleepers to non-sleepers directly supports the memory claim.

choices.text: the statement that the sleep-performance relationship appears to follow a curve
choices.rationale: The curve concerns amount, not the memory result itself.

choices.text: the statement that sleep may also clear away molecular waste from the brain
choices.rationale: Waste clearance is a separate benefit.

explanation: The strongest support is the experimental comparison of recall.

stimulus.title: The Night Shift of the Brain
stimulus.text: Sleep can look like idleness, but the brain is busy. During deep sleep, waves of electrical activity sweep across the cortex, and researchers think these waves help move the day's memories into longer-term storage. In one line of experiments, students who slept after studying a list of words remembered more of them than students who stayed awake the same number of hours. Sleep may also clear away molecular waste that builds up while we are awake. None of this means more sleep is always better; the relationship appears to follow a curve, with both too little and too much linked to poorer performance. What the brain seems to need is enough, at the right times.

prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that ice cores capture air from the distant past?

choices.text: the statement that the ice keeps no diary of dates
choices.rationale: Keeping 'no diary of dates' concerns dating, not capturing old air.

choices.text: the statement that each winter's snowfall does not entirely melt
choices.rationale: Snow not melting explains how layers form, not the captured air.

choices.text: the statement that the bubbles hold the very atmosphere that existed when the snow fell
choices.rationale: Correct. The bubbles holding the atmosphere of when the snow fell directly captures past air.

choices.text: the statement that drilling deep into the ice sheet is a way of drilling back through time
choices.rationale: The 'drilling back through time' image is a metaphor, less direct than the bubble detail.

explanation: Capturing past air is supported by the trapped-atmosphere detail.

stimulus.title: Bubbles of Old Air
stimulus.text: Each winter's snowfall on a polar ice sheet does not entirely melt; it packs down, traps tiny pockets of air, and slowly turns to ice. Layer settles on layer, year after year, so that drilling deep into the ice is a way of drilling back through time. Trapped in those bubbles is a sample of the very atmosphere that existed when the snow fell, including the gases it carried. By analyzing cores pulled from kilometers down, researchers can compare today's air with the air of tens of thousands of years ago. The ice keeps no diary of dates, yet its layers, counted carefully, let scientists assign an age to each whisper of ancient air.

prompt: Which quotation best supports the idea that Priya feels reluctance about her chosen move?

choices.text: 'She let the whole board blur'
choices.rationale: This describes her narrowing of focus.

choices.text: 'the pawn on the sixth rank was a promise'
choices.rationale: This describes her commitment to the pawn, not reluctance.

choices.text: 'her hand did not want to do'
choices.rationale: Correct. Her hand's unwillingness to give up the knight is the reluctance.

choices.text: 'Nine minutes left for her, fourteen for him'
choices.rationale: This states the time situation.

explanation: The personified hand that 'did not want to' is the expression of reluctance.

stimulus.title: Forty Moves
stimulus.text: By the thirtieth move, Priya had stopped seeing the pieces as pieces. The knight on the rim was a trapped thing with one way out; the pawn on the sixth rank was a promise she had made twenty moves earlier and now had to keep. Across the table her opponent, a boy in a sweatshirt who had not looked up once, took her bishop with an unhurried hand and pressed the clock. Nine minutes left for her, fourteen for him. Her coach's voice surfaced: when you are behind on time, do not think faster; think about fewer things. She let the whole board blur except for the pawn and the two squares in front of it. There was a path. It required giving up the knight, which her hand did not want to do, and she noticed, with something like amusement, that her hand had opinions. She moved the knight anyway. The boy looked up.

prompt: Which quotation best supports the idea that the camp is overcrowded?

choices.text: 'There are forty of us in a space meant for twenty'
choices.rationale: Correct. Twice the intended occupancy is a direct statement of overcrowding.

choices.text: 'The hills are brown and lie about in heaps'
choices.rationale: This describes the landscape.

choices.text: 'I am writing on the lid of a trunk by the light of a lamp that smokes'
choices.rationale: This describes his writing conditions, not the number of people.

choices.text: 'I had expected to be lonely'
choices.rationale: This describes an expectation, not the crowding itself.

explanation: The forty-in-a-space-for-twenty detail states the overcrowding outright.

stimulus.title: A Letter from the Camp
stimulus.text: Dear Margaret, You will forgive the hand; I am writing on the lid of a trunk by the light of a lamp that smokes. We reached the river camp on Tuesday, two days later than the captain promised and a full week later than Father feared, which puts the truth, as usual, somewhere between hope and worry. The country here is nothing like the engravings. The hills are brown and lie about in heaps, and the river is the color of weak coffee. I had expected to be lonely and find instead that I am never alone, which is worse. There are forty of us in a space meant for twenty. Still, this morning a boy no older than you showed me how to find water by watching where the birds go at dusk, and I thought: here is something I would not have learned at home. Tell Mother I am eating. It is nearly true. Your brother, Thomas.

prompt: Which quotation from the text best supports the idea that Ines's father has been unable to perform his usual duties?

choices.text: 'She trimmed the wick, polished the great lens until her own face swam in it'
choices.rationale: This describes her tasks without indicating why she performs them.

choices.text: 'the keeper's log ... now bore her looser script'
choices.rationale: Correct. The log he kept for twenty years is now in her handwriting, showing he can no longer keep it.

choices.text: 'counting them under her breath as her father had taught her'
choices.rationale: This shows he taught her, not that he is unable to work now.

choices.text: 'It was the only conversation she had ever had with strangers'
choices.rationale: This concerns her feelings about the beam, not her father's condition.

explanation: The handover of the log is the detail that directly shows the father's incapacity.

stimulus.title: The Lamp Room
stimulus.text: Every evening at dusk, Ines climbed the one hundred and twelve iron steps to the lamp room, counting them under her breath as her father had taught her. He was ill that winter, and the keeper's log, which he had kept in his cramped, careful hand for twenty years, now bore her looser script. She trimmed the wick, polished the great lens until her own face swam in it, and set the clockwork turning. Below, the sea worried at the rocks. Ines did not love the lighthouse, exactly; she loved the moment when the beam first swung out across the water and she imagined a ship's mate, miles off, lifting his head. It was the only conversation she had ever had with strangers, and it consisted of a single word, repeated all night: here.

prompt: Which quotation best supports the idea that Mrs. Abernathy has not been honest with her family?

choices.text: 'while the kettle screamed and nobody came to take it off'
choices.rationale: This describes her household's inattention, not her dishonesty.

choices.text: 'She had not yet decided whether she would get on'
choices.rationale: This is her indecision, not deception.

choices.text: 'the clock was wrong, which everyone in town knew and no one corrected'
choices.rationale: This is about the town, not her.

choices.text: 'The cousin existed; the fortnight did not'
choices.rationale: Correct. The two-week visit she described to her sister is a fiction.

explanation: The false fortnight is the lie.

stimulus.title: The Eleven-Forty
stimulus.text: The station at Harwell had two platforms and one clock, and the clock was wrong, which everyone in town knew and no one corrected. Mrs. Abernathy stood under it in her good coat with a hatbox at her feet. She had told her sister she was going to visit a cousin in the city for a fortnight. The cousin existed; the fortnight did not. In her handbag, beneath the gloves, was a letter from a music conservatory addressed to a Miss E. Abernathy, which she had not been for twelve years, and which she had opened at the kitchen table that morning while the kettle screamed and nobody came to take it off. The eleven-forty was late. It was always late, by exactly the amount the clock was wrong, so that it arrived, in a manner of speaking, on time. She picked up the hatbox when she heard it. She had not yet decided whether she would get on.

prompt: Which quotation best supports the claim that constant activity undermines thinking?

choices.text: 'Some of them will pay anyway'
choices.rationale: This concedes a payoff, not a harm.

choices.text: 'it starves the very faculty it claims to prize'
choices.rationale: Correct. Starving the faculty is the harm to thinking.

choices.text: 'I do not propose that anyone work less'
choices.rationale: This is a clarification of the proposal.

choices.text: 'Every hour is to be optimized, every habit tracked, every pause justified'
choices.rationale: This describes the culture without stating the harm.

stimulus.title: In Defense of Doing Nothing
stimulus.text: We have made an idol of productivity. Every hour is to be optimized, every habit tracked, every pause justified as 'recharging' for the work to come. Even rest is permitted only as an investment. I want to argue for something less respectable: time that is not for anything. The case is not sentimental. Most people can name the moment a stubborn problem came loose, and it was rarely at the desk. It was in the shower, on a walk, in the dull middle of a long drive. The mind does its deepest sorting when it is left alone, and it cannot be left alone on a schedule. A culture that fills every gap does not merely tire its members; it starves the very faculty it claims to prize. I do not propose that anyone work less. I propose that when the work is done, we stop pretending that the hours afterward owe us a return. Some of them will pay anyway. That is not why they are worth having.

prompt: Which quotation best supports the idea that the narrator's view of maps changed permanently?

choices.text: 'Mr. Hallam took the pen from my hand'
choices.rationale: This is the moment of intervention, not its lasting effect.

choices.text: 'It was my task that winter to copy the surveys sent back from the northern voyage'
choices.rationale: This describes the task.

choices.text: 'I have come to think of the gaps as the most honest lines on them'
choices.rationale: Correct. The present-tense reflection shows a lasting change.

choices.text: 'I was nineteen and thought this a modest ambition'
choices.rationale: This describes the earlier, unchanged view.

explanation: The closing reflection states the enduring change.

stimulus.title: The Unfinished Coast
stimulus.text: My master, Mr. Hallam, had drawn maps for the Admiralty for thirty years, and in all that time, he told me, he had never once drawn a line he had not been given reason to believe. I was nineteen and thought this a modest ambition. It was my task that winter to copy the surveys sent back from the northern voyage, and I came to a stretch of coast where the ship's log simply stopped: fog for nine days, then open sea. The chart before me showed a gap. I proposed to close it with a gentle curve, as any sensible coast would run. Mr. Hallam took the pen from my hand. 'A sailor who trusts that curve,' he said, 'will put his ship on rocks we have not seen, and he will do it in the dark, and he will do it because you were tidy.' He left the gap. I have since drawn a great many maps, and some of them have gaps, and I have come to think of the gaps as the most honest lines on them.

prompt: Which quotation best supports the idea that the philosophers did not dismiss external events?

choices.text: 'I had been grading myself on events in which I had no vote'
choices.rationale: This is the author's own error, not the philosophers' view.

choices.text: 'confusing the two is the chief source of unhappiness'
choices.rationale: This concerns the cost of confusion, not the value of external events.

choices.text: 'They did not say that the second category is unimportant, only that it is not ours'
choices.rationale: Correct. This states directly that the external category was not called unimportant.

choices.text: 'On one side are the things within our power—our judgments, our efforts, our intentions'
choices.rationale: This lists what is within our power, not the philosophers' view of the rest.

explanation: The sentence explicitly denies that the philosophers dismissed externals.

stimulus.title: What Is Ours
stimulus.text: I used to keep a list of things that had gone wrong that week, with the idea that reviewing it would make me wiser. It made me miserable instead, and I eventually understood why. Most of the items were not mine. The weather, a colleague's mood, the outcome of a vote in a city I had never visited: I had been grading myself on events in which I had no vote. An ancient school of philosophers drew a line that I have since found useful. On one side are the things within our power—our judgments, our efforts, our intentions. On the other side is everything else. They did not say that the second category is unimportant, only that it is not ours, and that confusing the two is the chief source of unhappiness. I still keep a list. It is shorter now, and every item on it is something I actually did, or failed to do. On bad weeks it is a harder list to read. On good weeks it is the only one that counts.

prompt: Which quotation best supports the idea that the siblings had anticipated difficulty with the smaller items?

choices.text: 'It was heavier than he remembered'
choices.rationale: This is Ben's final perception.

choices.text: 'They had agreed easily on the furniture, which neither wanted, and the photographs'
choices.rationale: This describes the easy part.

choices.text: 'had come, as they had both known they would, to the small things'
choices.rationale: Correct. 'As they had both known they would' shows the anticipation.

choices.text: 'It was the fourth hour'
choices.rationale: This shows duration, not anticipation.

explanation: The clause about knowing is the direct evidence.

stimulus.title: Division
stimulus.text: 'You take the clock,' Dana said. 'You always liked it.' 'I never liked it,' said Ben. 'I wound it because nobody else would.' They were sitting on the floor of their mother's apartment with the lists between them, hers typed, his on the back of an envelope. It was the fourth hour. They had agreed easily on the furniture, which neither wanted, and the photographs, which they would scan and share, and had come, as they had both known they would, to the small things: the clock, the chipped blue bowl, the cheap ring their mother had worn in place of the good one she kept in a drawer. 'Then I'll take it,' Dana said, and wrote it down, and Ben watched her write and felt, absurdly, that something had been taken from him. 'Or we could sell it,' she said, not looking up. 'No,' he said, too quickly, and they both heard it. She crossed it off her list. He picked up the clock. It was heavier than he remembered.

prompt: Which quotation best supports the idea that the adoption of standard time was not universal?

choices.text: 'the major rail companies divided the continent into four broad zones'
choices.rationale: This describes the creation of the zones, not their reception.

choices.text: 'some towns refused outright, keeping "sun time" as a point of pride'
choices.rationale: Correct. The refusing towns show that adoption was incomplete.

choices.text: 'most people had quietly agreed to let a company's timetable ... tell them what time it was'
choices.rationale: This shows widespread adoption, the opposite of the point.

choices.text: 'A traveler heading west ... could find the clocks a few minutes behind at each stop'
choices.rationale: This describes conditions before standard time existed.

explanation: The towns that kept sun time are the direct evidence of holdouts.

stimulus.title: Noon by Agreement
stimulus.text: Until the 1880s, noon in most American towns was simply the moment the sun stood highest over that town. A traveler heading west from one city to the next could find the clocks a few minutes behind at each stop, and nobody minded, because few people traveled fast enough to notice. The railroads changed this. A train running on a timetable built from dozens of local noons was a train waiting to collide with another. In 1883, the major rail companies divided the continent into four broad zones and declared that every clock within a zone would read the same. The federal government did not endorse the scheme for another thirty-five years, and some towns refused outright, keeping 'sun time' as a point of pride. But commerce followed the trains. Within a few years, most people had quietly agreed to let a company's timetable, rather than the sky, tell them what time it was.
